opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think distillation is best understood as one instance of a really general trend: once some capability exists at the frontier, the cost of reaching that same level of capability falls very quickly afterwards. Historically, if you look at a fixed level of performance on some benchmark, the compute or dollar cost to hit it has dropped by a large factor per year. Some of that is hardware, some is algorithmic progress, and a meaningful chunk is just that once you know something is possible, and you have a strong model available, it's much easier to get there.

Distillation is the most direct version of that. You have a big, expensive model, and you use its outputs, whether that's raw completions, reasoning traces, or its probability distributions over tokens, as training signal for a smaller model. The smaller model gets a much richer, denser signal than it would from just pretraining on internet text. It's being shown what good answers look like, and often how to get to them. So you can get a model that's maybe an order of magnitude cheaper to run while retaining a large fraction of the performance on the stuff you care about.

A few implications I think are important.

First, the frontier and the cheap tier are coupled. Improvements at the top flow down pretty fast, so if you're thinking about who has access to some dangerous or economically important capability, you shouldn't just think about who can train the biggest model. You should think about who can get access to that model's outputs, or to a model distilled from it, a few months later. That matters a lot for things like export controls or for model weight security. If you secure the weights but anyone can query the model at scale, a meaningful amount of the capability can leak out through distillation, though usually not all of it, and usually with some lag.

Second, it's not a free lunch. Distilled models tend to be somewhat narrower. They often match the teacher on the distribution they were distilled on but are less robust off-distribution, and they generally don't exceed the teacher. So distillation compresses capabilities rather than creating new ones. The thing that pushes the frontier is still mostly scale, better RL, better algorithms. But for deployment economics, compression is huge, because inference cost is what determines how widely something gets used.

Third, and this is more relevant to the things I worry about, cheap capabilities change the picture for AI automating AI research. If you can take a strong model and make it, say, ten times cheaper to run, you can run many more copies, run them faster, and do much more parallel work. A lot of the dynamics around how quickly AI R&D could accelerate depend on how much inference compute you need per unit of useful work, and distillation is one of the levers that pushes that down.

And then from a safety perspective, there are some open questions about whether properties you care about transfer through distillation. If the teacher has some subtle misaligned tendency, does the student inherit it? There's some evidence that various traits can transfer even through data that looks innocuous, which I think is a reason to be somewhat cautious about assuming a distilled model is "clean" just because you filtered the outputs. Conversely, you might hope to use distillation as a tool: take a model you have more trust in, or outputs you've carefully vetted, and train on those. But I wouldn't count on it as a strong guarantee.

So overall I'd say: distillation is a big part of why capabilities diffuse fast and get cheap fast, it means the effective lag between "the frontier lab has this" and "lots of actors have something close to this" is short, and it's an important factor in how fast things could move once AI systems are doing a lot of the work themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says the cost of reaching an existing capability can fall quickly and distinguishes compression from frontier progress, but it does not state that making a capability cheaper is easier than making it substantially better.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame distillation is that it's one instance of a pretty general phenomenon, which is that once you've figured out how to do something at all, doing it again is way cheaper than doing it the first time. And that's true across a lot of domains, but it's especially true in AI, because the "something" you've figured out is itself a kind of artifact that you can learn from.

So the basic picture is: you train some big, expensive model. Maybe that costs you a huge amount of compute, a lot of research effort, a lot of trial and error on the data mix, the architecture, whatever. And then once you have that model, you can use it to generate outputs — answers, reasoning traces, labels, rankings — and train a much smaller model on those outputs. And the smaller model often gets you a surprisingly large fraction of the capability for a small fraction of the cost.

And I think the reason this works is sort of intuitive once you say it out loud. The big model has already done the hard work of finding the right behaviors. The small model doesn't have to search for them; it just has to copy them. And copying a solution is a much easier learning problem than discovering it. The supervision signal is just much cleaner. Instead of "here's a bunch of internet text, figure out what matters," it's "here's exactly what a good answer looks like, do that."

So where this fits into the broader pattern — I'd say there are a few different mechanisms by which capabilities get cheaper over time, and they stack. There's algorithmic progress, where you just find better training recipes and architectures, and that compounds in a pretty steady way. There's hardware getting cheaper per FLOP. There's the fact that people figure out what data actually matters and stop wasting compute on stuff that doesn't. And then there's distillation, which is sort of a different kind of thing, because it's not that you've discovered a better way to learn the capability from scratch — it's that you're leveraging the existence of a model that already has it.

And I think the important strategic implication is that distillation makes capabilities diffuse much faster than you might naively expect. If the only way to get a frontier model was to replicate the frontier training run, then the gap between the leader and everyone else would be bounded by how expensive that run was. But if you can get most of the way there by distilling from the leader's outputs — which you often can, if you have API access, or even just access to the outputs that people post publicly — then the moat is a lot thinner than the raw compute numbers suggest.

I do want to flag some caveats, though, because I think people sometimes overstate this. Distillation is really good at transferring the capabilities the teacher already has. It's not good at exceeding them, at least not in a straightforward way. So it's a mechanism for catching up, not for pulling ahead. And it also tends to work better for some kinds of capabilities than others — things where the output itself contains most of the useful signal distill well, and things where the capability is more about some diffuse world knowledge or some very broad robustness tend to be harder to compress.

And then there's the question of what happens at the frontier specifically. I think the frontier labs are themselves using distillation heavily — you train a huge model internally, you distill it down into the thing you actually serve, because inference costs matter a lot. So in some sense the models people have access to are often already distilled, and then external actors distill from those. It's distillation all the way down.

The thing I'd keep coming back to, if I'm trying to think about what this means for how the next several years go, is that it pushes toward a world where capabilities proliferate quickly, where the lead a frontier developer has is measured in months rather than years, and where the thing that's actually scarce isn't "can you get a model that's roughly this capable" but "can you be the one who gets there first and has the most capable model at any given time." Which has pretty significant implications for how you'd want to think about safety, governance, who has access to what — all of that. But that's maybe getting ahead of the question.

r001.rationale: The response says reproducing an established capability is much cheaper and easier than discovering it, and describes distillation as catching up rather than pulling ahead.

astra-6.text:
I think distillation is one instance of a pretty general pattern where discovering how to do something is much more expensive than reproducing it once you know how. You might spend a huge amount of compute training a model that can solve some difficult class of problems. But once you have that model, you can use it to generate examples of successful solutions, and train a cheaper model on those examples.

The cheaper model doesn’t have to independently discover everything that went into the original capability. It gets a much more direct training signal: here are the kinds of answers you should produce, or here are the steps that lead to a good answer. And that can make acquiring the capability substantially cheaper.

There are limits. You shouldn’t assume that a small model can reproduce everything a much larger model does, or that doing well on the examples means it will generalise equally well. But the broad implication is that the cost of first demonstrating a capability can be quite different from the cost of deploying it widely. So when thinking about the impact of AI, I’d distinguish ‘How expensive is it to get this working for the first time?’ from ‘How expensive will it be to run once people have had time to make it efficient?’

r001.rationale: The response says reproducing a demonstrated capability can be cheaper than discovering it, but it does not compare making a capability cheaper with making it substantially better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think distillation is one instance of a pretty general pattern where producing a capability for the first time is much more expensive than reproducing it once you know how to do it.

You might spend a huge amount of compute training a very capable model, and then use that model to generate examples that a smaller model can learn from. The smaller model doesn’t have to independently discover everything the larger model discovered. It gets to learn from the larger model’s outputs, which can make acquiring some of those capabilities substantially cheaper.

There’s also a version of this with reasoning: you spend a lot of compute getting a model to solve a problem, and then train on successful solutions. You’re turning some of that expensive search into something the model can do more directly.

This doesn’t mean you can preserve every capability at arbitrarily low cost. But it does mean that the cost of first demonstrating a capability can be a pretty misleading guide to what it will eventually cost to deploy widely.

r001.rationale: The response explains how reproducing or deploying a demonstrated capability can be cheaper, but does not compare that with how difficult it is to make the capability substantially better.
